extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged public, reformers and readers interested in constitutional comparison between England and revolutionary France
extracted.subtask_description: A political pamphlet-argument comparing the French Constitution's principles with English practices, advocating specific constitutional and social reforms (representation, abolition of privileges, church/state separation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation proportional to taxable inhabitants/electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that the number of representatives for any place shall be in a ratio to the number of taxable inhabitants or electors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a standard against English anomalies (examples given: county of York ~1,000,000 souls sends two members; Rutland, much smaller, also sends two; Sarum with not three houses sends two members; Manchester with ~60,000 sends none). Commentary: current English distribution is capricious and needs further reform to achieve fair representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular, frequent elections (two-year terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that the National Assembly shall be elected every two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a democratic guard against corruption and entrenched power; contrasted with Burke's supposed reliance on precedent rather than principle. Implies accountability through frequent re-election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of game laws / landowner's right to wild game on his land
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says there shall be no game laws, that the farmer on whose lands wild game shall be found ... shall have a right to what he can take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as removing privileges that make game the property of those who do not feed it; an element of removing aristocratic legal privileges that hurt commoners.

rubrics_metrics.name: No monopolies; free trades and occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that there shall be no monopolies of any kind--that all trades shall be free and every man free to follow any occupation ... throughout the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolies criticized as aristocratical: chartered towns and electoral qualifications are described as monopolies. Examples: corporate chartered towns, restricted electorates (Bath: right of electing monopolized by ~31 persons). Anti-patterns: chartered monopolies that bar newcomers and restrict natural rights to acquire occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude government officers/placemen/pensioners from legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve the national representation from being corrupt, no member of the National Assembly shall be an officer of the government, a placeman or a pensioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a rule preventing conflicts of interest and 'loaves and fishes' corruption; aimed at preventing government influence and purchase of legislative loyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent conflict of interest in voting supplies (separation of payer and payee)
rubrics_metrics.description: If those who vote the supplies are the same persons who receive the supplies when voted ... they are themselves accountable to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The national purse should not be managed by those who both appropriate and receive funds; current English system likened to being both mortgagor and mortgagee. Anti-pattern: ministers and MPs who both vote and benefit from supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of war and peace resides in the nation (those who pay the expense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says that the right of war and peace is in the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: those who bear the cost should decide on war. Critique of English practice where the right is effectively in the Crown or ceremonial symbols. The constitution also separates (1) right to declare war (nation), (2) expense (nation), and (3) mode of conducting (executive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place sovereignty in the nation, not the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The third article of the declaration of rights says: 'The nation is essentially the source (or fountain) of all sovereignty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with English notion of king as 'fountain' descended from conquest; supports idea that representative institutions should originate from the people, not royal grant or patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative supremacy: law before the king ('la loi, le roi')
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution puts the legislative before the executive, the law before the king; la loi, le roi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must exist before execution; the phrase is invoked as the natural order. Implies executive officers act under law, rather than law being subordinate to the monarch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the king as official from sovereignty in the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power ... is in the hands of a person styled the King; but the French Constitution distinguishes between the King and the Sovereign: It considers the station of King as official, and places Sovereignty in the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats the monarch's role as an office-holder rather than the source of legitimacy; supports republican accountability while retaining an executive function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of titles
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution says, 'There shall be no titles'; titles are called nicknames that mark 'a sort of foppery' and degrade personhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: titles are meaningless, create social division, and should fall away by popular contempt or formal abolition; society should ground rank in character, not titular distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of primogeniture / end inheritance-based aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: To restore parents to their children ... and to exterminate the monster aristocracy, root and branch--the French Constitution has destroyed the law of Primogenitureship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primogeniture presented as unnatural, unjust (disinheriting younger children), socially costly (publicly funded sinecures), and the legal root of aristocracy; abolition is advocated to restore family equity and social health.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hereditary legislators / rejection of a hereditary peerage
rubrics_metrics.description: Because there is an unnatural unfitness in an aristocracy to be legislators for a nation ... a body of men, holding themselves accountable to nobody, ought not to be trusted by anybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple grounds offered: aristocracy corrupts ideas of justice, continues conquest-based principles, tends to degenerate by inbreeding, and creates a class not accountable to the public. France rejects a House of Peers; hereditary legislature seen as absurd and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate clergy incomes to reduce extreme inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution has reformed the condition of the clergy. It has raised the income of the lower and middle classes, and taken from the higher. None are now less than twelve hundred livres ... nor any higher than two or three thousand pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a corrective to glaring inequalities between high beneficed clergy and poor curates; invoked as part of broader social justice reforms (Burke's comparison criticized as misframed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish tithes (end tithe system)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution has abolished tythes ... When land is held on tythe ... the farmer bears the whole expense, and the tythe-holder takes a tenth of the improvement ... the farmer gets less benefit for improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tithes treated as an inequitable regime that disincentivizes improvement and burdens farmers; abolition is a constitutional remedy to restore fairness between producers and tithe-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Right of Conscience (abolish 'toleration' as a legal category)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Constitution hath abolished or renounced Toleration and Intolerance also, and hath established Universal Right Of Conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: 'toleration' is itself a presumption of authority (granting or withholding liberty) and is therefore a form of despotism; true liberty of conscience is an inherent right, not a government concession. The state must not interpose between man and his Maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of church and state / no law-established religion
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the continual choruses of Mr. Burke's book is 'Church and State.' ... By engendering the church with the state ... a sort of mule-animal ... called the Church established by Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established religion is blamed for persecutions (Inquisition, burnings) and for corrupting religious institutions into instruments of oppression and state profit; separation is recommended (example: America as proof of benign coexistence without establishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should spring from the people's inherent right, not royal grant
rubrics_metrics.description: The representatives of the nation ... originate in and from the people by election, as an inherent right in the people. In England it is otherwise ... the Parliament ... was erected by patents from the descendants of the Conqueror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes democratic origin of legislative bodies as a constitutional principle; criticizes English origins of Parliament as grants from crown/patent rather than delegated right of populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary speech and privileges are inherent, not permissions from the king
rubrics_metrics.description: The President of the National Assembly does not ask the King to grant to the Assembly liberty of speech ... Speech is, in the first place, one of the natural rights of man always retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing parliamentary free speech as a duty and right stemming from election and nation-authority, not as a concession the monarch can grant or withhold; contrasts with English practice where addresses seek king's favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part approach to war: declaration, expense, conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: On this question of war, three things are to be considered. First, the right of declaring it: secondly, the expense of supporting it: thirdly, the mode of conducting it after it is declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French model: declaration and expense in the nation, conduct left to the executive. Presented as a blueprint to reduce propensity to war and align decision-making with those who bear costs.
